children: The U.S.-Venezuela oil agreement strengthens the outlook for Venezuela's sovereign debt restructuring and supports higher oil production, although key details remain unclear, a Morgan Stanley report published on Tuesday said.

The U.S. and Venezuela unveiled an arrangement last week under which private company North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) would receive a 100-year concession covering 17 oil fields with an estimated 65 billion barrels of reserves.
As part of it, the U.S. government would obtain a 35% equity stake in the company's parent, rights to purchase 20% of future output at cost and first refusal on the other 80%.

Morgan Stanley maintained its base case that production will rise to about 1.5 million barrels per day by the end of 2027, a level it believes would support a successful restructuring of the country's massive pile of defaulted debt.

Venezuelan sovereign bonds and those of state oil company PDVSA have already gained around 3.5% since news of the U.S. agreement emerged last week, reflecting a potentially more favourable economic outlook ahead of restructuring discussions.

Morgan Stanley's analysts said the significance of the oil announcement lay less in the specifics of the deal and more in what it signalled about Washington's commitment to Venezuela and the wider Western Hemisphere.
"The announcements are a positive for sovereign bonds even though many more details are still needed, especially on the fiscal impact," the report said.

The plan's aim to invest up to $100 billion in Venezuela's aging oil infrastructure could materially boost production if realised, but the report also cautioned that many details of the plan and its financing were still lacking.

More broadly, the deal represents a dramatic expansion of the U.S. role in Venezuela's oil industry. The country holds the world's largest proven oil reserves but produces only about 1.25 million barrels per day, far below its potential after years of underinvestment, mismanagement and sanctions.
